A soldier using an acoustic amplifier system to detect the sound of approaching aircraft. Bolling Field, Washington, D.C. 1921

These acoustic locating devices usually consisted of large horns connected to the operators' ears using tubing, much like a very large stethoscope.

The first use of this type of equipment was claimed by Commander Alfred Rawlinson of the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, who in the autumn of 1916 was commanding a mobile anti-aircraft battery on the east coast of England. He needed a means of locating Zeppelins during cloudy conditions and improvised an apparatus from a pair of gramaphone horns mounted on a rotating pole.

As World War II neared, radar began to become a credible alternative to the sound location of aircraft and these devices became obsolete during the War.

Card with A

Card with D Card with 4

Card with 7

You can flip more than one card.

You flip card A, see an odd number. Hypothesis is false.

You flip card A, see an even number. You have failed to falsify the hypothesis.

You flip 7. If it has a vowel on the other side then you have falsified the hypothesis.

You flip 7. If it has a consonant then you have failed to falsify the hypothesis.
